explanations.explanation: Paul says it plain: “…you should have commended me…” He says they drove him to being a fool, so a little credit was in order. I'd want a pat on the hat myself in that spot.

That's a fair guess, friend, but it's not the word Paul uses. He says they should have commended him, since he is in no way inferior to those “super-apostles.” He's asking for credit, not a correction.
Warning is a good-sounding word, but Paul doesn't say it here. What he says is that they "…should have commended…" him. Think of a guy who does all the work and gets a shrug instead of a thank you.

Yes, friend, that's true. Paul says he is “…in no way inferior…” to those super-apostles, which is a bold thing to say. Then in that same sentence he adds, “even though I am nothing.” A big claim and a humble one, all in one breath.
Not quite, friend. Paul writes, “…I am in no way inferior to those “super-apostles…”…” He says it flat out. Right after that he adds, “even though I am nothing.”
That's the list, baker. Paul says “…signs, wonders, and miracles…” were performed among them. He adds that they were done with great perseverance. The Corinthians were right there among it.

Those sound like they could belong, but they're not the ones Paul names here. In verse 12 he says the marks of a true apostle were “…signs, wonders, and miracles…” That's the trio, so keep it in your pocket.

Those are good things, friend, but Paul doesn't list them in this verse. Fasting and prayer didn't make this list, and I would have bet my apron on them too. What he says is that “…signs, wonders, and miracles…” were performed among the Corinthians.

Yes, baker. Paul asks, “In what way were you inferior to the other churches, except that I was not a burden to you?” So the one difference he names is that he didn't burden them. Then he adds, “Forgive me this wrong!” I think that line has a twinkle in it.
Close, but read it again. Paul asks, “In what way were you inferior to the other churches, except that I was not a burden to you?” He names exactly one exception. It's that he didn't burden them.

explanations.answer: He wants them and not their things
explanations.explanation: That's it, friend. Paul says, “…I am not seeking your possessions, but you.” He's not coming to collect. He's coming for the people, and I'd take that guest over the one who eyes my cookie jar.

explanations.answer: He has plenty of money saved up
explanations.explanation: The text never says that, friend. Paul's reason is this: “…I am not seeking your possessions, but you.” His money isn't the point. The Corinthians are.

explanations.answer: He plans to stay only a short time
explanations.explanation: Paul says nothing about how long he'll stay. His reason is “…I am not seeking your possessions, but you.” That's what keeps him from being a burden.

Right, baker. Paul says, “For children should not have to save up for their parents, but parents for their children.” The saving goes from parents to children. Just before that he says he is “…not seeking your possessions, but you.”
That one's flipped, friend. Paul says children “…should not have to save up for their parents…” He says it's “…parents for their children.” Turn it around and you've got it.

Paul doesn't bring brothers and sisters into this one, friend. Nobody's splitting a cookie jar between siblings here. He says, “For children should not have to save up for their parents, but parents for their children.” So the saving goes from parents to children.
Yes, friend. Paul says, “…I will most gladly spend my money and myself.” He's not only opening his wallet, he's giving his whole self. That's a big gift, and he says he gives it most gladly.
Good try, but that's not in the verse. Paul says he'll spend “…my money and myself.” He gives himself, not just his name, and he does it "most gladly."
A house is a big thing to give, and I'd have guessed it too. But Paul doesn't mention one. The verse says, “…I will most gladly spend my money and myself.” Not a deed or a key in sight.
Not this time, friend. Paul doesn't say "grudgingly." He says, “…I will most gladly spend my money and myself.” Gladly, and most gladly at that.
You've got it, baker. Paul says, “…I will most gladly spend my money and myself.” That's the opposite of grudging, and it's for the sake of the Corinthians' souls. He's happy to pour it out.

That's him, baker. Paul urged Titus to go visit them and sent another brother along too. Elsewhere he calls Titus his partner and fellow worker (2 Corinthians 8:23). Then Paul asks, “Did we not walk in the same Spirit and follow in the same footsteps?”

Timothy is a name that fits in this neighborhood, since he's named alongside Paul at the start of this letter (2 Corinthians 1:1). But in this passage Paul says, “I urged Titus to visit you…” So the name you're after is Titus.
Silas is a real traveling partner of Paul's, the one he chose in Acts 15:40. But he's not the name in this passage. Paul says, “I urged Titus to visit you…”
Not quite, friend. Paul says, “I urged Titus to visit you, and I sent our brother with him.” So Titus didn't go alone. Paul sent a brother along too.
That's it, baker. The verse says, “I urged Titus to visit you, and I sent our brother with him.” So Titus had company. Paul doesn't name the brother, so I won't either.

explanations.answer: Titus acted just as Paul did
explanations.explanation: Right, baker. Paul asks, “Did we not walk in the same Spirit and follow in the same footsteps?” Same Spirit, same footsteps. That's his point about himself and Titus.

That's not what Paul says, friend. He asks, “Did we not walk in the same Spirit and follow in the same footsteps?” His point is that he and Titus walked alike. Nothing about a separate plan is in the verse.
The text doesn't say that, baker. Paul's question is, “Did we not walk in the same Spirit and follow in the same footsteps?” His point is that they walked alike, not that one replaced the other.
Yes, friend. Paul says, “We speak before God in Christ, and all of this, beloved, is to build you up.” He's not on trial. He's building. And he calls them beloved while he does it.
Paying back isn't what Paul says, friend. He says all of this “…is to build you up.” That's his purpose, and he says it speaking before God in Christ.
Sorting things out sounds tidy, friend, but those aren't Paul's words. He says, “…all of this, beloved, is to build you up.” I'd take a messy bakery full of builders over a tidy one any day.

Yes, baker. Paul says, “…I am afraid that when I come, I may not find you as I wish, and you may not find me as you wish.” So the worry runs both ways. I think he knows the visit could be a bumpy one.
Look again, friend. Paul says, “…I may not find you as I wish, and you may not find me as you wish.” So he does worry about how they'll find him. The worry goes both directions.

That's on the list, baker. Paul says, “I fear that there may be quarreling, jealousy, rage, rivalry, slander, gossip, arrogance, and disorder.” You picked three of the eight. He fears they may be there when he comes, and every one of them is about how people treat each other.

Those are hard things, but they're not what Paul lists. He says, “I fear that there may be quarreling, jealousy, rage, rivalry, slander, gossip, arrogance, and disorder.” His list is about how people treat one another.
Those feel heavy, friend, but Paul doesn't name them. His list is “…quarreling, jealousy, rage, rivalry, slander, gossip, arrogance, and disorder.” Every one of those is about how people get along.

That's the word, baker. Paul says, “I am afraid that when I come again, my God will humble me before you…” It's a fear, not a sure thing. He adds that he will be grieved over many who have sinned earlier.
Honor would be a nicer fear to have, friend. But Paul says, “…my God will humble me before you…” The word is humble, and it comes with grief.
Strengthening is a good thing, but Paul doesn't say it here. He says, “…my God will humble me before you…” That's what he fears, and he says he will be grieved.

Yes, baker. Paul says he'll be grieved over many who “…have sinned earlier and have not repented…” To repent means to turn from it, and he's grieved because they haven't. I think that comes from a heart that loves them.

Giving did come up earlier in this passage, friend, so I get why your hand went there. But Paul says he will be grieved over many who “…have sinned earlier and have not repented…” That's the word, and I think it's the one that weighs on his heart. Right neighborhood, wrong house!
Gathering isn't what Paul says here, baker. He fears he will be grieved over many who sinned earlier and “…have not repented…” Repented is the word, and it's a heavy one.
